title: On-call rotation: rules of engagement
excerpt: How we run the rotation, what counts as paged, when to escalate, and how we keep the on-call humane.
body_html:
The on-call rotation is the team's promise to itself: when something breaks at 2am, exactly one person owns the page, the response, and the comms — and everyone else gets to sleep.

Schedule

We run a follow-the-sun schedule with primary, secondary, and a manager-on-call. Shifts are seven days long and rotate Mondays at 09:00 local.

What counts as paged

Anything that fires through PagerDuty or a customer-impacting incident reported in #incident channel within 5 minutes counts as paged.

Escalation ladder

  1. Primary acknowledges within 5 minutes.
  2. If no ack in 5, secondary is paged automatically.
  3. If still no ack in 10, manager-on-call is paged.
  4. Manager-on-call has authority to escalate to incident commander.

Keeping it humane

No single engineer should be on-call more than one week in four. Comp time after a rough rotation is mandatory, not optional.

title: Postgres primary failover — quick reference
excerpt: Five-minute walkthrough for promoting the replica, drafting a comms blurb, and verifying replication caught up.
body_html:
Use this when the primary is degraded and you need to fail over to the streaming replica.

Pre-flight

  • Confirm replica lag < 10 seconds in Datadog.
  • Page the database lead in #db-oncall before doing anything irreversible.

Promotion

Run: pg-failover promote replica-1 --confirm

This takes ~30 seconds. The promote drops the existing primary out of the cluster and updates the connection-string secret in the vault.

Comms

Draft a one-paragraph status update, post to #incident, and set the status page to partial outage until the new primary has caught up on writes.

title: Parental leave: the policy and the spirit of it
excerpt: Sixteen weeks paid, flexible ramp, no pressure to return early. Here is exactly how to take it.
body_html:
We offer sixteen weeks of fully-paid leave to all parents — birth, adoption, or foster — with no minimum tenure.

Letting your team know

A simple Slack message in the team channel is fine. Your manager helps draft a coverage plan; you do not need to do it yourself.

Ramp back

The first month back is a 60% ramp by default. Adjust up or down with your manager.

Questions

People Ops holds office hours every Thursday at 2pm. Anything you want to ask in private goes to people@example.com.

title: Q4 pricing RFC — usage-based tiers
excerpt: Proposing a shift from seat-based to usage-based pricing for the platform plan. Open for comment until Friday.
body_html:
Status: Draft · open for comment until 2026-05-03.

Summary

We propose moving the platform plan from seat-based to usage-based pricing. The unit is active workspaces per month.

Why now

  • 38% of platform revenue is bottlenecked by seat caps that don't reflect actual usage.
  • Three of our top-10 customers have asked for usage pricing in the last 60 days.

Open questions

  1. Migration path for existing seat-based contracts.
  2. Floor / ceiling pricing to avoid surprise bills.
  3. How to communicate the change without scaring the long-tail.

title: How we communicate during incidents
excerpt: Status page cadence, customer comms templates, and what NOT to say in the first 30 minutes.
body_html:
The first 30 minutes of an incident are about acknowledging, not explaining. Resist the urge to speculate on cause.

Cadence

  • T+0: status page set to investigating.
  • T+15: first customer-facing update (even if it just says "we are investigating").
  • T+30: every 30 minutes thereafter until resolved.

What not to say

  • Never speculate on root cause publicly until the postmortem.
  • Never blame a vendor in customer-facing comms.
  • Never give a fix ETA you are not 90% confident in.

Templates

Pre-approved templates live in the incident-comms Slack canvas. Use them; don't write fresh copy under pressure.

title: Design tokens v2 — the migration plan
excerpt: We're moving from a flat token list to a layered architecture (primitive → semantic → component). Here is the plan.
body_html:
We are moving from a flat list of design tokens to a layered model: primitive → semantic → component. This document covers the migration plan and the timeline.

The layers

  • Primitive — raw color/space/size values. Never used directly in components.
  • Semantic — --color-action-primary, --space-stack-md. Used by component CSS.
  • Component — --button-bg, --card-padding. Used inside one component only.

Timeline

Q2: ship the primitive layer + semantic mapping. Q3: refactor the top-20 components onto component tokens.

title: Warehouse schema conventions
excerpt: How we name tables in the analytics warehouse, and the rules around fact / dim / staging layers.
body_html:
The warehouse is split into three schemas: staging (raw + lightly-cleaned), core (the modelled layer), and marts (consumer-facing tables).

Naming

  • staging: stg_<source>__<table> (e.g. stg_stripe__charges).
  • core: dim_* for slowly-changing entities, fct_* for facts.
  • marts: business-team prefix (finance_*, growth_*).

Ownership

Every table in marts must have a named owning team. The owner is responsible for the SLA on freshness and for fielding questions.
